reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A late-onset four-repeat tauopathy, largely affecting the very elderly, that often presents with slowly progressive amnestic decline and prominent neuropsychiatric or behavioural features
Named for the spindle- or comma-shaped argyrophilic grains that stain with silver and with tau in the neuropil, especially in the limbic system
Emotional and personality changes, irritability and, at times, features overlapping with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia may be disproportionate to the memory deficit
It is frequently found alongside Alzheimer disease and other age-related pathologies at post-mortem, complicating clinical attribution
The disorder tends to progress more slowly than typical Alzheimer disease and is often relatively mild
There is no specific biomarker in life, so it is largely a neuropathological diagnosis made after death
Recognition matters mainly for understanding the substrate of late-life amnestic and behavioural syndromes and for research classification
reference.pathophysiology: Argyrophilic grain disease is an age-related sporadic tauopathy characterised by deposition of abnormal four-repeat tau protein as small argyrophilic grains within neuronal processes, together with coiled bodies in oligodendrocytes and tau-positive pretangles in neurones. The pathology has a predilection for the limbic system, particularly the medial temporal lobe, amygdala and adjacent structures, which underlies the amnestic and neuropsychiatric features. Because it commonly coexists with Alzheimer disease and other age-related changes, its independent clinical contribution can be difficult to isolate, and it is regarded as one of several tau pathologies contributing to cognitive impairment in the very elderly.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive supranuclear palsy and other four-repeat tauopathies
additionalInvestigations: Neuropsychological assessment to characterise the amnestic and behavioural profile
MRI of the brain, which may show medial temporal atrophy without distinguishing features
FDG-PET to assess the pattern of cortical metabolism
Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers to assess for coexisting Alzheimer pathology
Exclusion of reversible causes of cognitive and behavioural change
Neuropathological examination, which remains the definitive diagnostic method
redFlags: Rapid cognitive decline inconsistent with the usually indolent course
Severe behavioural disturbance compromising safety in an elderly patient
Features suggesting a coexisting or alternative rapidly progressive dementia
New focal neurological signs requiring further investigation
reference.prognosis: Argyrophilic grain disease generally follows a slow and relatively mild course compared with typical Alzheimer disease, though coexisting pathologies often influence the overall trajectory; management is supportive, addressing cognition, mood and behaviour.
pitfalls: Assuming all late-life amnestic decline is due to Alzheimer disease when argyrophilic grain pathology may contribute
Overinterpreting non-specific medial temporal atrophy as diagnostic
Failing to recognise that mixed pathology is the rule rather than the exception in the very elderly
Attributing prominent behavioural change solely to a primary psychiatric disorder
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying therapy, so management is supportive and symptom-directed
Trial a cholinesterase inhibitor for cognitive support, particularly where coexisting Alzheimer pathology is likely, reviewing benefit

Manage neuropsychiatric and behavioural symptoms with non-pharmacological strategies first, using antidepressants or antipsychotics cautiously and sparingly for refractory agitation, mood disturbance or irritability
Exclude and treat reversible contributors to cognitive decline including metabolic, medication, mood and sensory causes
Provide structured dementia care with caregiver education, safety planning and advance-care planning
Support the patient through memory or old-age psychiatry services with occupational therapy and social care
Review cognition, mood and function regularly given the generally slow course
